statement: In healthy volunteers tested in laboratories, MDMA compared with a dummy pill (placebo) given to the same people on another day, double blind and in random order, is associated with higher self-ratings of feeling loving and friendly and of feeling for people shown in photographs (emotional empathy), but not with better recognition of other people's emotions, which was worse for fear in both studies that found a change: people felt warmer without reading others better. Certainty: low. Status: replicated (two independent teams; the comparison with methamphetamine and the money game rest on one study each). In Chicago, 21 healthy adults aged 18 to 38 (9 women) who had used ecstasy at least twice (15 times on average; 13 fewer than 10 times) each had four sessions at least 5 days apart, in random order: MDMA 0.75 mg/kg, MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, methamphetamine 20 mg and placebo (study conditions), sitting alone in testing rooms (Bedi et al., 2010). After MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, ratings of feeling loving (F(3,57) = 5.04, p = 0.004) and friendly (F(2.7,51) = 6.81, p = 0.001) were higher than after placebo in the 20 people with complete ratings, but they were not significantly different from those after methamphetamine, and only methamphetamine significantly raised the rating of feeling sociable (F(2.5,47.7) = 3.06, p < 0.05); MDMA 1.5 mg/kg and methamphetamine both raised playfulness, and MDMA 0.75 mg/kg raised loneliness (chi squared(3) = 11.94, p = 0.008). The means appear only in small figures on a scale whose range is not stated, so the size of these feelings cannot be given, and a non-significant difference from methamphetamine in 20 people shows neither that the feelings are the same nor that they differ; 6 of the 21 guessed they had taken ecstasy when they had been given methamphetamine. In a task with faces shown for half a second at strengths from barely to fully expressed, people named 0.55 of fearful faces correctly after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg against 0.63 after placebo (t(20) = 3.94, significant after correction for multiple comparisons), and 0.59 after both MDMA 0.75 mg/kg and methamphetamine, neither of which differed significantly from MDMA 1.5 mg/kg or from placebo; happy, sad, angry and neutral faces, complex emotions read from the eyes and emotions in voices did not change significantly by the authors' account (for voices, the printed F(3,57) = 3.01 would give p of about 0.04 before any correction, editors' calculation), and an exploratory, uncorrected analysis found more emotional faces called neutral after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg (51.71 against 44.90). The same laboratory's earlier study of 9 volunteers, whose faces were clearly expressed and shown for 4 seconds, found no change in the accuracy or speed of recognising them (Bedi et al., 2009, from its study card; the faces as described by Bedi et al., 2010). In Basel, 32 healthy adults (16 women; mean age 25), 22 of them new to MDMA and 10 with fewer than five earlier uses, took MDMA 125 mg (1.89 mg/kg on average) and an identical placebo at least 10 days apart (study conditions; random order is stated in the abstract only) (Hysek et al., 2014). Ratings of feeling happy, open and close to others rose (see the answer on what MDMA feels like). Three hours after the capsule, ratings of how much people felt for, and were stirred by, people in emotional photographs rose (explicit F(1,31) = 6.05, p = 0.019; implicit F(1,31) = 4.29, p = 0.047), significantly for scenes with positive emotions and not for negative ones; explicit ratings averaged about 5.0 after MDMA against 4.4 after placebo on a 1-to-9 scale (editors' reading of Figure 2A), while inferring the mental state of the people in the photographs (cognitive empathy) did not change (about 62% correct in both). Two hours after the capsule, accuracy in naming emotions in moving faces fell overall (F(1,31) = 28.63, p < 0.001), for fearful (14.90) and angry (18.60; both p < 0.001), disgusted (5.81, p = 0.022) and surprised (9.79, p = 0.004) faces but not happy faces (0.27, p = 0.607). Four hours after the capsule, in a money-allocation game in which two participants drawn at random were paid what they earned, a measure of how often people chose the split that gave the other person most rose (F(1,31) = 4.42, p = 0.044; an angle of about 37 against 31 degrees, editors' reading of Figure 3A). Plasma oxytocin rose (F(1,31) = 19.84, p < 0.001), but its rise did not correlate with the empathy or money-game changes. The empathy and money-game rises were significant in men and not in women on post hoc tests, and the fall in face-recognition accuracy in women and not in men, in 16 people per sex among dozens of uncorrected tests, so these sex differences are not established; the authors state that most volunteers realised which treatment they had been given, which may have biased task performance. The two teams read their results differently, the Basel authors as more emotional empathy and more prosocial behaviour, the Chicago authors as more social approach rather than more empathy; across the two studies, people felt warmer but did not read others better. These were single doses given by researchers to healthy, screened volunteers, with photographs, recorded voices and a money game in place of conversations with real people; nothing here measured empathy or behaviour towards people outside a laboratory.
plain: Does MDMA really make you more empathic? In lab studies, healthy volunteers took MDMA on one day and a dummy pill on another, without being told which. On MDMA they rated themselves more loving and friendly, and said they felt a bit more for people in emotional photos (about 5.0 against 4.4 on a 1-to-9 scale); the rise was clear for photos of positive scenes, not negative ones. But they did not get better at reading other people's emotions. In one study, people named 55 in 100 briefly shown fearful faces correctly after MDMA, against 63 in 100 after the dummy pill; in another, they got worse at naming fear, anger, disgust and surprise, while happy faces were read as well as before. In the study that also gave meth, MDMA's loving and friendly ratings were not clearly higher than meth's, and only meth clearly raised feeling sociable. Oxytocin, a hormone linked to social behaviour, rose on MDMA, but how much it rose did not match the changes in empathy. In a money game with real payouts, people on MDMA more often picked the split that gave the other person the most; the rise showed in the men, but with 16 men and 16 women that may be chance. These were small lab studies of 9 to 32 people, with photos, recorded voices and a money game rather than real conversations, and in one study most volunteers could tell they had taken MDMA.
population: Healthy, screened adults in laboratory studies: 21 in Chicago aged 18 to 38 (9 women; mean age 24.4) who had used ecstasy at least twice (mean 15 occasions; 13 fewer than 10), tested alone; 32 in Basel (16 women; mean age 25, range 20 to 31), 22 new to MDMA and 10 with fewer than five earlier uses; and, from an older study card, 9 in Chicago (7 men, 2 women) with earlier ecstasy use of 2 to 300 occasions
exposure: A single oral dose of MDMA in a capsule given double blind by researchers (study conditions: 0.75 and 1.5 mg/kg in Chicago in the 21-person study; 125 mg, 1.89 mg/kg on average, in Basel; 0.75 and 1.5 mg/kg in ascending order in the 9-person Chicago study), with tasks about 1 to 4 hours after the capsule
comparator: A dummy pill (placebo) in the same people on another day (random order stated in the Methods of the 21-person Chicago study and in the abstract only in Basel; placed at random among ascending doses in the 9-person study); in the 21-person Chicago study, also methamphetamine 20 mg in the same people as an active comparison
outcome: Self-ratings of feeling loving, lonely, playful and sociable (visual analogue scales) and friendly (Profile of Mood States); ratings of feeling for, and being stirred by, people in emotional photographs (emotional empathy) and percent correct in inferring their mental state (cognitive empathy); accuracy in naming emotions in briefly shown morphed photographs of faces, in eye regions and in voices (Chicago) and in moving faces (Basel); choices splitting money between oneself and another person, with real payouts to two participants drawn at random; plasma oxytocin

(2010), Chicago, 21 people (20 for self-ratings and voices), peak change from baseline, repeated-measures analyses with Bonferroni-adjusted follow-ups: loving F(3,57) = 5.04, p = 0.004, eta squared 0.21 (MDMA 1.5 mg/kg above placebo); friendliness F(2.7,51) = 6.81, p = 0.001, eta squared 0.26 (MDMA 1.5 mg/kg above placebo and above MDMA 0.75 mg/kg); MDMA 1.5 mg/kg against methamphetamine 20 mg not significantly different for either (no statistic printed); sociable F(2.5,47.7) = 3.06, p < 0.05, eta squared 0.14 (methamphetamine above placebo only); playful F(3,57) = 8.57, p < 0.001, eta squared 0.31 (MDMA 1.5 mg/kg above placebo and MDMA 0.75 mg/kg; methamphetamine above placebo); lonely chi squared(3) = 11.94, p = 0.008, r = 0.54 (MDMA 0.75 mg/kg above methamphetamine and placebo). Faces, proportion correct, mean (SD), placebo, MDMA 0.75 mg/kg, MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, methamphetamine: fear 0.63 (0.07), 0.59 (0.12), 0.55 (0.10), 0.59 (0.10), F(2.8,56.0) = 4.45, p = 0.008, eta squared 0.18; placebo against MDMA 1.5 mg/kg t(20) = 3.94 (significant after Bonferroni correction), placebo against methamphetamine t(20) = 2.59 and MDMA 1.5 mg/kg against methamphetamine t(20) = 1.31 (not significant); happy 0.74, 0.71, 0.71, 0.73 (F(3,60) = 0.96); sad 0.51, 0.54, 0.47, 0.52 (3.60); angry 0.64, 0.63, 0.59, 0.63 (2.0); neutral 0.69, 0.68, 0.77, 0.67 (2.84), none significant after correction; emotional faces called neutral 44.90, 46.52, 51.71, 46.48 (F(3,60) = 3.25; placebo against MDMA 1.5 mg/kg t(20) = 2.52; both p < 0.05 uncorrected, exploratory); Eyes test total 26.81, 26.67, 26.10, 27.24 (F(3,60) = 0.58); voices (DANVA-2, n = 20) 18.05, 18.00, 17.20, 18.70 (F(3,57) = 3.01, reported as no effect of MDMA; editors' calculation: p about 0.04 from the printed degrees of freedom, before any sphericity correction). Money game (Social Value Orientation angle) 4.42 (p = 0.044), by sex 5.52 (p = 0.026), post hoc men p = 0.008, women not significant; editors' reading of Figure 3A (degrees, placebo then MDMA): all 31 and 37, women 37 and 37, men 26 and 37; inequality-aversion index F(1,20) = 3.39 (p = 0.079; participants with a prosocial orientation only). Face accuracy, all emotions 28.63 (p < 0.001), by sex 6.04 (p = 0.020; women p < 0.001, men not significant); fearful 14.90 and angry 18.60 (p < 0.001), disgusted 5.81 (p = 0.022), surprised 9.79 (p = 0.004), happy 0.27 (p = 0.607); detection threshold for fearful faces 4.92 (printed P < 0.032). risk_of_bias.note: Randomized within-person comparisons with a dummy pill, at some concerns on the cards for MDMA against placebo: sc_bedi_2010 (RoB 2 some concerns: randomization not described, partial blinding, 5 of 15 visual analogue items and 1 of 8 mood subscales reported, no registration); sc_hysek_2014 (RoB 2 high overall because of its sex-specific post hoc findings, some concerns for the comparisons with placebo: random order stated only in the abstract, most volunteers realised which treatment they had, dozens of uncorrected tests); sc_bedi_2009 (high: ascending doses and selective reporting). The feelings are self-ratings by people who could often tell what they had taken; face accuracy is a performance measure less open to expectation. One level, not two, because the fear finding rests on that performance measure in two laboratories.

inconsistency.note: Where both teams measured the same thing they agree: fear was recognised less accurately after MDMA in Chicago (static faces shown for 500 ms) and in Basel (moving faces), and no emotion was recognised better in either; the earlier Chicago study, with clear faces shown for 4 seconds, found no change, which its authors attribute to a less sensitive task. Which other negative emotions fell differs between the tasks, and the statement says so. 'Sociable' rose only after methamphetamine in Chicago while 'close to others' rose in Basel; these are different items, and the statement rests on neither.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: laboratory tasks with photographs, recorded voices and a paper money game, and single doses given by researchers to healthy volunteers, as the statement says; it claims nothing about conversations or behaviour outside a laboratory.

imprecision.note: 20 to 32 people per study; the empathy and money-game results lie near the threshold (p = 0.019, 0.047 and 0.044, uncorrected), the sex-specific tests rest on 16 people each, and the comparison with methamphetamine in 20 people was not significant either way, so it cannot show that the feelings are alike or that they differ. No confidence intervals are printed (editors' calculation for the Chicago fear difference: 0.04 to 0.12).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: the Basel study was registered (records not read) and the Chicago study was not; selective reporting of subscales is counted under risk of bias.

grade.reasoning: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled within-person laboratory studies start high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give low; evidence that starts high is not upgraded. Low applies to the statement as a whole: self-rated loving, friendly and emotional-empathy feelings rose against a dummy pill, while recognition of other people's emotions did not improve and recognition of fear worsened. The fear finding alone would be moderate (two independent laboratories, a performance measure, t(20) = 3.94 and F(1,31) = 14.90); the money-game rise and the comparison with methamphetamine rest on one study each, would be low to very low alone, and are worded as single results. Status replicated: the Chicago (de Wit) and Basel (Liechti) laboratories are independent and agree in direction on fear recognition and on warmer self-ratings, measured with different items; the 9-person Chicago study comes from the same laboratory as the 21-person one and is not counted as independent. The size of the Chicago feelings cannot be given (figures only, scale range not stated); the Basel sizes are editors' readings of vector figures. The general mood and closeness ratings belong to the answer on what MDMA feels like and are not repeated. Kirkpatrick et al. (2014) was not used: its only finding on closeness, a difference between sites, is already in that answer. No advice on amounts or use is given; doses are study conditions.
